utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in public session, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I resume, I should like to say that my associate who is sitting in the gallery has informed me that yesterday, with the exception of the five minutes -- first five minutes of cross-examination, everything was in private session, and as you will remember, we had quite a bit of time in open session. So probably it continued in private session by inertia. And I wish to draw attention to this matter because there are many questions that can be asked in open session and were asked in open session yesterday. However, everything with the exception of the first five minutes was in private session. Not a single word could be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll check to see if he's right. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now continue in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. B-050, I should like to ask you, without identifying you personally, I should like to ask you something about the JNA before the outbreak of the conflict. You did your compulsory military service in the JNA, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The unit in which you served consisted of how many men? How many men were in this unit? This was several years prior to the beginning of the war, as I can see from your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the first time I served?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean when you did your regular military service. I won't even mention the year. But you indicated that in the second paragraph of your statement. When you did your national military service in the JNA in the SFRY, everything was peaceful and so on. Tell me, how many men were there in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you're referring to the first part, the first six months or the second six months?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring to both. Let me ask you first about the first six months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A 30-men platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a part of a unit, isn't it, of the institution in which you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many such platoons were there in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Ten or so. Very well. When you completed your first six months, you acquired a certain rank, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the lowest non-commissioned officer rank in the army, isn't it, the rank you obtained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it customary after the first six months, and once you acquire this lowest rank of a non-commissioned officer you are transferred and then you act as a platoon leader or commander? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope this is nothing confidential. There are tens of thousands of officers in reserve, so you cannot be identified on that basis.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. As a platoon leader, you had some 20 men under you. You were a sergeant. You had some 20 men in the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in the second part of my military service, I had two platoons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you were the leader of two platoons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, between 60 and 70 soldiers and eight corporals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was probably because there was a shortage of officer cadres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it customary, having completed this school of officers in reserve, the sergeant should be a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, what is the difference between your position after mobilisation and after the outbreak of the conflict from the position you held before in the army upon the completion of your regular military service? Namely, what I have in mind is that later on when you were mobilised again you had some 20 men under you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were again a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not an instructor. You were a platoon commander in the Territorial Defence of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The difference is that I was not mobilised by the JNA but by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But we established yesterday that this was part of the Territorial Defence of Krajina. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had the TO of the army and the TO of the police. And for me, it would have been more logical in those days to have been recruited by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what would have been more logical to you, but I am talking about the formation, the unit. Is that in accordance with the rank and position you would have normally held? So you were a platoon commander in the Krajina police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, do you say that you were some sort of an instructor? Every platoon commander in any military establishment trains those 20 men under him and attends military training with them. Is that customary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in that camp, the ranks of the JNA were not important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But surely the qualifications were. You were qualified to command a platoon during your regular military service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but of the Yugoslav People's Army, not of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the police that you were mobilised into in the service of the defence of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no difference regarding the training or was there any difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing the reserve officers' school during the second part of your military service with the soldiers under your command, did you undergo the same training that you underwent later on when you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similar or identical; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there anything specific about this second mobilisation as compared to the first? Regular training of the mobilised recruits by officers who had completed some kind of school prior to that, in this case the reserve officer school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any big difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I just wish to specify this. You were a platoon commander in the Krajina police. Why then mystifying the whole matter by talking about instructors or trainers, about a special status when there was no such thing? It was regular training.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mystify anything. I told the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it regular training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't regular when we were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't regular because we had been mobilised to the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us leave that aside for the moment, whether you had been mobilised to the army or the police, because as far as I know in Krajina in those days, both the army and the police --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the problem, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point of all this? Where is it taking anybody to spend minutes, if not parts of hours, arguing whether he was an instructor or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point, Mr. May, is that the opposing side is mystifying the position of this witness by abusing protective measures and using private sessions to present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not right. The point seems to be a totally trifling one without significance. I speak for myself, of course. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just one more question in this connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, it says that when you left the army before the war, when you were doing your national service and were for six months in the troops as a platoon commander that you left the army with the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not lieutenant, second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is -- do you know, because I also went to that reserve officer school, you first have the rank of sergeant and only later do you acquire the rank of second lieutenant and not lieutenant? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you're right, but I don't think it's important. I know that shortly afterwards, whether it was a month later, I acquired the rank of either second lieutenant or first -- lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you say that you specialised later on. Later you specialised in anti-aircraft weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not later. It was during my military service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were in the reserve officers' school of the air defences, the SPA, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was your regular military service in which you were trained for an office in reserve of the anti-air defences. So this point regarding rank is not correct, nor is what you said about specialising later correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Milosevic, what you are conveying, but I don't think there is any mystery about that. Everyone knows how these things function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on then. Yesterday you made a problem out of a question put to you in the examination-in-chief as to how much time you had spent in that camp, logor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a logor or "camp."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you why you are so sensitive about the word "logor"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was never in a "logor" and there is a difference between a "logor" and a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what the difference is between a logor and a camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that a logor means detainees, and a camp is people who are there on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know that the interpreter did not make any mistake, because camp is an English word and logor is our word? It's the same concept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't answer my question why you're sensitive to the word "logor."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sensitive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned arrests of Croats in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't arrests. It was in an operation. It was in action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, in action. And what were you, taking prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were exchanged on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were exchanged the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone mistreated among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they badly treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any order on the part of your superiors in the Territorial Defence or the police to respect the rights of prisoners of war and to take care not to make any infringements? Did you abide by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any case when someone did not comply with those rules, that mistreated prisoners or executed prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, personally, am not aware of any such case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, with precision. You spoke about April 1991 and the organisation where you attributed a role to Franko Simatovic, and you yourself said that you only saw Franko Simatovic in June 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he could not have had any connection with your original mobilisation or organisation or the composition of the police to which you had been mobilised. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as his physical presence is concerned, you're right, but I'm not aware of the political decisions that may have been taken earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And when did you see Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: September 1991. Well, then let's describe what you referred to in your examination. What was Stanisic at the time? You said that above Stanisic was the minister of the police, and he said on a couple of occasions that he would see the boss, and you think that he was referring to me and so on. So what was he then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a head of the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the point, Mr. B-050. Stanisic was not nor could he have been head of the state security of Serbia. In September 1991, that was not the position he held.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may have been right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you to say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how did that occur to you? I don't think he introduced himself falsely.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know that he became that shortly afterwards. If he wasn't then when we met for the first time, he became that shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if that was not his position, he con have acted in that position regardless of what he became later on. It's no doubt that he did become that later on, but at that time that was not the position he held.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask if we can to go into private session. I would like to answer this question in somewhat greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. B-050, tell me this, please, did you ever hear that Frenki Simatovic told you or anybody else or ordered you or anybody else, in fact, ordered ever, and I'd like to stress the word "ever," or suggest that you perpetrate a crime of any kind or an offence of any kind at any point in time as far as you know, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And along with what is considered professional training, was the basic idea that was the background of the training to defend one's country and one's people and nothing more than that? Is that what you were communicated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We most certainly are not going to -- stay in open session for that. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it true that your prime duty in the camp in which you spent almost five months was to train others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in that camp there weren't many recruits and that men came in small groups; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that they stayed for roughly a period of 20 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That they attended training for about 20 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May 1992? But you were there only until the end of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when you're asking me about these people who came and stayed briefly, this happened in May. But as for those who came earlier on, they stayed for longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one left while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said in your statement: "We knew that they wouldn't stay with us. And I was not at all interested in where they would go after that." Is that right what you said earlier on in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was translated, but what I just said is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that you knew that they wouldn't stay with you and that you had no interest as to where they would go after that. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said a moment ago is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it true that those people who came came without weapons, and they left your camp again without weapons? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right that they returned to their villages and then they continued working and training other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this second period, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that it is only once they arrived there in the villages did they receive weapons from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct what is also stated in your statement, I quote: "I that the Red Berets that we trained probably were implementing the orders of local municipal leaders in Bosnia or perhaps of the Crisis Staffs." Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right. And could this be in private session, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see no reason why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only this last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the reason for there, Mr. Nice? I'm not sure that I follow. It's like the earlier question we had. It really seems to me to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can only infer that the source of information to which the witness would refer could identify him, but I would respectfully suggest that the Chamber might wish to ask the witness that himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the difficulty, Mr. B-050, about this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am thinking only of this last question when Mr. Tapuskovic is asking me about the Red Berets, the beginning of the Red Berets and the men coming and going. Only this question mentioning the Red Berets. Everything else is okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mention anything specific. I am just saying the Red Berets. That in itself cannot reveal your identity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session. It's matter which we're going to have to return to. It's not a satisfactory situation, but at the moment I can see no alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you speak about the events at the Miljevacka plateau. Can you explain to Their Honours what happened on that plateau? Was this an attack that occurred during a period of cease-fire or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that the Croatian side attacked even though there was a cease-fire? That 50 men were killed of which 20 were innocent civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours how the innocent civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a Croatian armed operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind. I'll withdraw. I'll withdraw that question. When those events started in the spring of 1991 and when that unit was formed, was the population already on the move and were there already a large numbers of Serbs who were fleeing Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you think they fled? They were leaving Krajina going to Bosnia or Serbia or Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly the Serbs were leaving who were living in towns with a majority Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this after this operation in 1992 at the Miljevacka plateau, did Serbs again leave those areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In smaller numbers. In that period, yes, in that region yes, everyone left. In that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you say sometime in March 1993 there were about 5.000 Serbs in Knin from the area of Zadar. Had they fled from Zadar and moved to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you followed developments in the period that followed, and that will be my last question, how many refugees were there from the Krajina? How many people left their homes in those areas? Right up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-050 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately between 100 and 200.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we in open session? We are. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are in open session at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's stay there as long as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Dealing with the issue of the taking of the statement. The position was broadly as I was reminded it was when I mentioned it before the adjournment. At the interview, the investigator had his own tape machine and I think notes. On review, the tape provided nothing audible even with enhancement techniques. The witness was then brought to The Hague and the statement was then taken from him in more detail here, so that there is nothing audible that could be disclosed to the accused. I have one more passage of the statement that I must read to you, but I must seek leave to do that in closed session. It arises from a question of Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In open session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to go into open -- do you want to go into private session now or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll try to deal with everything in open session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Okay. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer if question, please, just yes or no, Witness B-050, just yes or no: Were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think I can ask this question safely in open session but we can come back to it. May we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can start -- we can be in open session, can we, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes. Could we have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask the declaration be read to the witness and he assent to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the interpreters would read the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would just stand. Mr. Witness, if you can hear us. A declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- Is going to be read to you. If the interpreters would assist. Just a moment. It may be if you would read it in English, Mr. Groome, that maybe the way to get at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If the usher would hand it to me. Quoting: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please, Mr. Witness? Start again, Mr. Groome? Would you just take the document and just read the first phrase, and if the interpreters interpret it and then, Mr. Witness, if you would repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one phrase at a time. Now, Mr. Witness, you're going to hear through your earphones a phrase, and it's the declaration that you will tell the truth, and we need to hear it before we can begin your evidence. What is going to happen is that counsel will read it out phrase by phrase. You will hear it repeated, and it will be for you then to repeat it to us. Let's try. Just the very first phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly -- I'm repeating as you said it. Yes. Yes, I do. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "The whole truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English? Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "And nothing but the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will be tendering a binder of exhibits. We ask that a number be assigned at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecutor's Exhibit 430.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that we begin by showing the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit 430, tab 1. Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd ask you to look at the name on the top of that sheet and ask you do you recognise that as your own name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout these proceedings, I and other members in Court will refer to you as B-1701. Sir, I'd ask you to begin your testimony here by describing for the Chamber in a few sentences about the village of Glogova in the municipality of Bratunac. Can you please tell us approximately how big is Glogova, and what was the ethnic make-up of that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: As to the ethnic composition, it was complex and everything was very good. We all cooperated very well, and there were no problems there at all. And there were 750 inhabitants of the village of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that Glogova was the second largest community in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to April of 1992. Did there come a time when you observed large numbers of uniformed soldiers coming into the village of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please answer that question? Did there come a time in April of 1992 that you saw large numbers of uniformed soldiers in the vicinity of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please give the Chamber some idea about the quantity of soldiers and describe how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: You want me to tell you how many soldiers there were? Well, I wasn't able to count them, but there were a lot of them. There were a lot of APCs and tanks, people in uniform wearing the JNA uniforms, all of them. There weren't any other type of uniform. And that was around the fountain and down to the out-patients' department as well, the health centre. On each corner and in front of every house there would be a soldier and a woman, a female.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: And they all had their rifles cocked. On the buildings, at the windows, up on the fountain I saw a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to ask you a bit more specific -- a few more specific questions about the uniforms. You described them as being JNA uniforms. Was there anything else that some of these soldiers were wearing that appeared to you to be not part of the standard JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I wasn't able to notice anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The fountain is, in fact, the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you've mentioned seeing some APCs, armoured personnel carriers and tanks. Can you approximate for the Chamber how many tanks you saw and how many APCs you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Approximately 10 to 15 vehicles that I saw there where I walked past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to a period after that. Did there come a time when the president of your local community of Glogova informed you and other villagers that you needed to come to the community centre to hear a speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the president of your local community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Nezir Ibisevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to the local community centre as you were instructed to do by him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, were you addressed by somebody who you knew regarding the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us in a sentence or two the substance of what Miroslav Deronjic told you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: He told us that we were to take down all the hunting rifles and to hand them over, that we shouldn't panic, and that our hunting rifles would be returned to us eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any assurances to you and the other people there at that time that you would not be harmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask to connect to the second microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They're asking for the second microphone to be turned on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, sometime after you heard the speech by Mr. Deronjic did you have a conversation with a person by the name of Ramo Ibisevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in substance what it was you and Mr. Ibisevic discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I went to the shop, which is where Ramo Ibisevic's son was working. I wanted to take some goods. Ramo arrived. There were some six or seven of us. And he said to us -- he said, "This evening I saw a truck going by on the macadamised road up to the bridge, and the person was handing out weapons. They were all machine-guns and that type of weapon." That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he specify the ethnicity of the people that were receiving these weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: He didn't tell us anything with respect to the ethnicity. He didn't see anything. But it was at the Magasici village and that he saw Miroslav Deronjic there, he was there, and all this was by Magasici village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Magasici village, what was the ethnic composition of that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: It's the local community of Glogova. Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Was there a predominant ethnic group in that village in Magasici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: It was half/half. There wasn't -- half/half. Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime after that was there another meeting in front of Mehmed Ibisevic's house with respect to the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you orient us with respect to the time? What's your best recollection of when this second meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Roughly, I can't tell you exactly, but about four days prior to the burning of the village. Three or four days before the village was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who addressed you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic spoke to us. He came to the gates of the schoolyard. He said, "Don't be afraid. No need to panic." Some people asked questions, and he said, "Your -- you want to kill us with our own rifles," and he said, "No," and that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person you're describing as Deronjic, can you summarise for us what you knew him about him, what position he held or what you knew about him at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I don't know his position or anything like that. I just knew him when he was a child and when he went to school, when he was a schoolboy. I knew him very well then and I knew his father too. We were all friends and I can't say anything on that score. We were all friends. Later on he went to school, and what happened afterwards, I don't know. And I never knew what position he occupied, what post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you actually did surrender your weapon or members of your village did in fact surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, we did surrender the very next day. We surrendered our weapons by Ibisevic's house, next to Ibisevic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly who you surrendered these weapons to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly, but there were three or four policemen. One of them was wearing civilian clothes, and they issued permits. But there was no stamp on the permit or anything like that, and nobody could read --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Receipt, sorry. Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you and others handed in their weapons, those people were given a receipt to show that they had surrendered their weapon; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, shortly after this event, did you come to realise that Glogova had been surrounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. When we handed over our weapons, it was already surrounded Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the tanks, with the APCs, and the army. And there was shooting from all sides. But they didn't shoot at the people. They shot up into the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon your observations that day, would it have been possible for you or other members of your village to leave the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We were so excited and upset. We didn't know what to do with our lives. That's the state we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that surrounded your village at this -- at this stage, were you able to see what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe in a sentence or two what you recall about what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't see the army, but we saw the tanks and such like. All of them were wearing the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything that they were wearing that was out of uniform as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't understand your question. What is it you're asking me? Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see two tank drivers, and if you did, could you describe what if anything they had on their head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. It's clear to me now. I did see those two tank drivers from the waist up. They stood on the asphalt road. They got out and talked with the people that were around them, and I saw the cockades and the wide sort of caps that they had on their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: With the five-pointed star on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later that evening did you watch a news programme from -- broadcast from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go in the proper order. When we handed in our weapons, we were surrounded. I went home. Then there was shooting all around. A bullet whizzed by. They were shooting into the air. And then they left. Now, whether the army had left from the hills, I didn't see, but the tanks and the transporters, the APCs, left. And I was watching the Belgrade news programme. They were praising us in Glogova, that we were the best people, that we had handed in our weapons as we should have. However, the next day they attacked us and killed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say the next day. Are you able to recall with precision the day that the village was attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I remember very well. I can never forget that for as long as I live. On the 9th of May, in the morning, at 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe your observations at 6.00 a.m. that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I woke up. I heard shooting. And as houses were burning, I ran out of the house. I got frightened. All the houses were burning except the two next to mine. And I turned into my maize field and I reached a small thicket. I lit a cigarette. They came up to my house, set fire to it and moved on. I stayed there and they went on. They set fire to all the houses. The hay, whatever could burn, they set alight. Then they came back in line, and they were approaching me. And they said, "Don't hurt him. Give him over to me." My house was burning. We stopped there. He wouldn't let me sit down or anything. He kept me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a few specific questions about this event. Prior to waking up that morning, was there ever any armed resistance or any conflict of any sort in the village of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to a group, and you've read to as "they." Can you please tell us as best you're able how many people were in this group and if you would describe what you recall about they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Like the fire brigade uniforms. That uniform is what they wore. And they were carrying some incendiary material. They must have been using some inflammable solution, because that is how they set the houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing anything to cover their faces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this: For a moment don't deal with the -- just a moment. Just a moment, please. Just assist us if you would. You refer to "they" all the time. They were doing this in the village. They were setting fire to the houses. Who was it that you're referring to, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army. The army. I'm sorry. That's what I meant. That is the words I use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many members of the army did you see on that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: That morning when they came back towards me and caught me, I couldn't count them. They were surrounding me and going right down to the commercial centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing anything on their faces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No. I didn't see them anything. But those people who came up to me, they had -- were masked with stockings over their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that morning, did you hear an explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard an explosion, but I didn't know where it came from until Ibisevic Mehmed told me that it was his house right next to the mosque across the road, and a hand-held grenade was fired and this hit the minaret of the mosque and destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, while you were hiding in your cornfield, did you make observations of what this group was doing at the houses of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: They weren't doing anything. Whoever they found in the house they would chase out and force them to go towards the commercial centre, and the others would follow and start the fires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you or put to you the name of some of the people who lived in the area, and I'd ask you to comment briefly on what you observed about what happened at these individual houses. The first home I'd like to ask you is the home of Medo Delic. Did you see what happened at Medo Delic's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: From up there as the soldiers came through the houses -- Medo Delic was a sick man. He was 60 years old, and he was a pensioner. They found him. They forced him out, and they started to beat him. They forced him about 10 metres from the house, and they were slapping him. And then one of them just killed him with his gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I draw your attention now to the house of Seco -- the home of Seco Ibisevic. Can you describe what if anything you observed occur at that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I saw another group which was coming towards Ibisevic Seco's house. There were three women in that group. And they called Seco out. He came out in front of his house as well as his wife Zlatija. They started mistreating him. I couldn't really hear very well because it was quite a long way from me. But I had a view across the meadow. They asked him, "Where is your son, Nezir, president of the local community?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the house -- the home of Adem Junuzovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Adem Junuzovic's house. They chased him towards -- they chased them towards Adem's house. And when I was forced out -- and I saw some blood right up to Adem's house. They also forced Adem out of the house and into a meadow 10 or 15 metres away. They separated Adem and Zlatija to the right and Seco to the left. Then the women were there. They cursed, and then they killed Zlatija and Adem with a pistol. And to the left of where Seco was there was a machine-gun was used. And I saw him sitting in a ditch, as if he were still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now you've just referred to some women. The women that you're referring to in your last answer, were they members of the village that was under attack or were they members of the group that attacked the village, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: They were with those soldiers who had attacked the village, and they were also wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you saw Seco sitting there, were you able to tell whether he was alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: He was dead, but he looked as if he was alive. That was the position he had in the ditch. He was in a seating position -- sitting position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were taken into custody by this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: This group of men -- a second group of men came that were forming the encirclement. There were those next to Seco's house. They were the groups inside that were searching the houses and capturing people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness now be shown Prosecution Exhibit 430, tab 2. Sir, while this exhibit is being brought to you, did there come a time when you assisted an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor for that investigator to draw a map of the area where the events you've described today occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is exhibit -- tab 2 in front of you a copy of that map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after you were taken into custody, where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Very took us towards the shopping centre. On the way there, I was escorting my mother, holding her by the arm. I do apologise. And then they said, "Go up there to Mujo's house." There was a trailer. They were gathering the men there. He started beating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself beaten, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. On the head with a -- the handle of an axe, and with a pick, the handle of a pick on our backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point in time, the people who were doing these things, did they appear to you to be part of the same group that initially attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I couldn't notice. They were soldiers, anyway, wearing JNA uniforms. With stockings over their head you can't recognise anyone. And we weren't even allowed to look to the side. We were told to look at a pillar, at Mujo Osmanvic's house. If anyone turned his head, he would get a bullet in the back of his head or in the temple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After being taken into custody, did you ever see Miroslav Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I saw him right there where we were. Actually, when we were going, he was at the bus station in front of the house of -- I'm sorry. I've forgotten the name now. Zaim Emanovic's house -- Beganovic, rather. He was standing at the station with a couple of men. He didn't say anything. We passed on. And up there, as I have already said, they mistreated us. Then he would come again after that. He turned his car around at Mujo Osmanvic's house and returned back. I didn't see him again while we were there. Then they lined us up on the asphalt. We were kneeling in various positions, and we had to look at this pillar of Mujo Osmanvic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: And then they took us back. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in front of Mujo Osmanvic's house, were the men from the group separated from the women in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this point in time, were you able to identify any of the people perpetrating this, doing this, as being members of the community, of the local Serb community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: You couldn't recognise anyone. They had these socks on their heads. They all wore the same uniforms. There was nothing to distinguish them by. We couldn't recognise them, nor were we allowed to look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you witness the beating of Nezir Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you also present when his son was taken away to be beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you saw or observed Nezir Omerovic being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe your observations regarding that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I personally saw when they took Nezir once down there to Dzafo's house and when they brought him back again twice. Then they left him there. Then they took his son two times. No. I'm sorry. The second time, he didn't come back again. They killed him in front of Dzafo Delic's house. Then Nezir was ordered to go towards Mujo's house. He hadn't made 2 or 3 metres. There was a burst of fire, and he fell on his stomach dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Camil Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him on this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. He was brought there in a wheelchair. He was next to me, right next to the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: He was half in the wheelchair and half leaning against the wall. And then a woman said, "Camil, where do you want me to shoot you, here or here? In the back or in the head?" There were two bullets in the back, and the third bullet in his head, and his nose was blown off. And then she jumped over someone. I can't remember who it was. Mensur's nephew who had brought him in the wheelchair, she killed him too. No one else fired except her. I didn't really see her kill him. As she turned around towards me, she raised her pistol up into the air and it was still smoking. Then she took off the mask from her face. She took a bottle of brandy from another soldier, and she drank two or three -- an amount equal to three fingers from the bottle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time when you were ordered with a number of other men to collect some of the dead bodies and bring them somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. Others continued killing people, and we were then ordered to carry the dead in front of Dzafo Delic's house. We reached Dzafo Delic's house, and they said, "Take it to the river. Take them to the river." Then the soldiers lined up as if they were going to a cemetery to carry the dead. They were lined up up to the river, and then we carried them there and we threw them right into the water. That's what we had to do. And then we were ordered, me and some others, to carry some more. And we headed towards there to carry those dead, and just then Nezir and Selmo Omerovic hadn't thrown one into the river properly, and then someone cursed him and said, "Throw him into the river." He bent down to throw the body in and he was shot at and killed. Then Ibisevic Jusuf was standing in front of me, and he said -- he asked Jusuf for money, and Jusuf says, "I gave whatever I had up there on the road. I have nothing else. Surely, neighbour, you wouldn't kill me. We went to school together," I think he said or something like that. I'm not quite sure about that. "Surely you're not going to kill me. I have two small children."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: "You know yourself I am an invalid."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some more specific questions about the carrying the bodies down to the river and about this area you've just got into. How many bodies were carried down on this first trip to the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Up to the river two of us would carry one body, so I really don't know how many. We were out of our wits. We were terrified. And we carried those bodies and threw them into the river. Then we came back again a second time, and that is when I saw Deronjic. And Jusuf said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm going to interrupt. Of course it's difficult, but, witness, can you try and give us some idea of how many bodies you carried and were carried altogether to the river.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I carried two bodies myself in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And can you give us any idea of how many others bodies were carried to the river, a rough idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We all carried two -- two bodies each twice. Twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many men carried these bodies on these two trips?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I can't tell you that, because we didn't dare look left or right, nor do I know that exactly, how many of us there were. There were 27 in that group, that -- I know that for sure. Now, I came back a second time with a group. Then Camil was left Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. alone up there. And after he was brought there in a wheelchair with Memisevic and his crutches and Omerovic's crutches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've mentioned observing a number of people being killed up until this point. My question to you is: Were any of these people that you could see --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Were any of these people armed or were they offering any type of resistance to the people that were attacking them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No one had anything, no weapons, nor did they show any resistance. How could they? They didn't have any weapons. There would be no sense in doing that anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention once again to what happened to Jusuf Ibisevic. You began to describe a conversation that he was having with another person. Can you please identify, if you're able, the other person he was speaking with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this point in time were you able to see what Miroslav Deronjic was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, I could see. He was wearing a uniform, an officer's uniform of the JNA, and a beret on his head, slanting to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have anything concealing his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you summarise for the Chamber what of that conversation you could hear between Mr. Ibisevic and Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Jusuf turned to face him and say, "Neighbour, are you really going to kill me? I have small children. Can't you see that I am disabled?" That is what I saw him say. And then this soldier killed Jusuf, firing three shots into his chest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: And all the other people were shot in the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're saying a soldier shot Jusuf. Was that Deronjic or was that another person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't Deronjic. A soldier who had a mask over his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while this soldier shot Jusuf, did Mr. Deronjic do anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No, nothing. He just stood there. He didn't react at all. And later on when I went up there to fetch the second group of people, he was gone. I didn't see him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us already about carrying a second set of bodies to the river. After that period of time, did you also see some bodies in front of a person's house by the name of Dzafo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Dzafo Delic, yes. I saw between seven and ten dead bodies, including Nezir's son right next to the fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just in a summary fashion tell us the type of injury that you observed on those bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Their heads had been blown up. Nezir's son's head was okay. He was lying on his back. You could see his face, he wasn't shot in the head. His face was okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these dead bodies that you saw at this point in time, were they men or women or a combination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: All men. They were all men that were killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about a person in a wheelchair, Mr. Camil Rizvanovic. Did there come a time when you carried his body down to the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Ibisevic, no. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not Ibisevic. Mr. Camil, the man in the wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Camil Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his body carried down to the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: His body was carried later on. When we brought the second set of bodies, we were lined up close to the river. And then they said, "You're going up to the meadow past these dead." And then we left turned and as I turned I saw Ramiz Cosic. I was the first and he was the second. He was up to here. And as I turned around, his head disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, so that we can better understand your evidence, after the second -- you participated in bringing the second group of bodies to the river, were you lined up along the river with some other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: We weren't lined up. You mean those who were killed on the road up there? Is that what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to -- did there come a time when you were asked to stand by the riverbank or stand and face the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other men were in the group with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: There were ten of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what happened --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Actually, there were eight of us because they had killed Selmo and Jusuf. So there were eight of us. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. Of the men that were lined up with you facing the river, did you know any of these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I only knew this Ramiz Cosic and Dzafo Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what happened after you and the other men were lined up facing the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: What happened was that we were lined up facing the river, and they said, "You go up towards those meadows." And the order came, turn left, and they opened fire on us. And as I turned around and Ramiz Cosic's head disappeared. Then these others fell over me. I fell over the others into the water in the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Later on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this shooting, were you injured in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you were fired upon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Nothing. What could I do? I was completely beside myself. I was unconscious. I didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe precisely where it was that you landed or ended up after the men shot at you and the other group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: We fell into the river over the other corpses. I fell this way, to my right side. And just this part of my nose was above water, and this ear. The rest of me was in the water. And Rizvanovic's brains had splattered across my neck. And I was among the dead myself, the dead bodies myself. And I was like that for four full hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in the river at that point for four hours submerged except for your nose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. All except the tip of my nose and my left ear. And I began to get cramps, and I was feverish. I had no more strength left in me. I thought they were going to kill me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what, if anything, you recall about what happened during that four hours that you lie partially submerged in the riverbank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I was lying in the river, in the water, and I was wondering whether I should raise my head to see if there was anybody around, to whether I could try and hide. And I looked across the bank and towards Dzafo Delic's house and the asphalt road I saw some people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear shooting continuing during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, I could. There's a small creek, a brook nearby. This brook was nearby, and on the other side of the brook they had lined up some people and shot them, and there were 25 people in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during that period that the body of Camil, the man in the wheelchair, was discarded into the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. I said a moment ago. I mention this had a moment ago. Mehmed Ibisevic brought Camil in his wheelchair. And as I said, his brains were splattered across my neck. And when I got up, I saw that there was a piece of brain lodged in the neck of my shirt. And they said they were supposed to go up across the meadow up there. And he was swearing at him. I don't know what he said, but he said, "You thought you would survive the genocide and then flee to be a witness." And he shot at him. And just here on the right-hand side there was a piece of his shirt that was left intact. Otherwise, all the rest was blown to smithereens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you believed it was safe to move from the water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No, it wasn't safe because the army was close by. You could hear them shouting. They would say, "Here he is," and then there'd be shooting. They'd shoot at the houses. But it was high time for me to leave the water. And I got up, and I looked across and saw somebody round a tree trunk. I moved towards him. I wasn't looking at him. And I thought, well, if he shoots, he shoots. But this was a man called Saban. I knew him. He was a driver. I knew his brother too. And I said, "Well, Saban, I've just been two metres away from you. Why didn't you tell me to get up?" And I said, "Let's go off, Saban. We'll go up to the houses, get to there. We can't stay here either." And I was all feverish at the time. I was going to fall down, but I managed to stand up. We went there. The other group was killed. And I was wondering whether my son was among them. He was with the young guys there. No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son die on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No, he didn't. My son died later on in Konjevic Polje. He was killed by a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient place to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Witness B-1701, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Would you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a just a few more questions about what happened at the river. Were you aware that other men were killed in a similar way to the men around you at the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe any other killings that you have personal knowledge about that occurred by the river on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Well, that other group when they brought them above the brook, the brook a little way up from us, the command was, "Aim, fire. Turn to the left, aim, and fire," and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many people were in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Twenty-five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us -- were they men and women or one or the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: All of them men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give the Chamber some idea about the approximate ages of this group of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: From 30 -- 18 to 30 years old. Thirty would be the eldest in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people that escorted them down to the river, were you able to see how many people did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I saw them. I raised my head to have a look, to see whether I should leave or not. Then I looked towards the left. There were the 25 people, and four of them, four soldiers, with their automatic rifles cocked at the ready, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the other men in your group when they were shot at, were any of them dressed in uniforms of any type? I'm talking about the victims now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No. No, they weren't, no. No, nobody had a uniform. Where would they get one from? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of those men armed in any way that you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No, nobody was. Just the hunters, they had. But nobody else had any weapons, no, no. Before, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The group of 25 men, I want to ask you the same two questions. Can you just describe were they in civilian clothes or uniforms, and did you see any indication to you that any of those men were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: No. No. They were all wearing civilian clothes. Of course they didn't have any uniforms, just civilians. They were all young. Fourteen years, 30 years old was the oldest one, and a man with his two sons. And he was lying there with his -- embracing his two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in preparation of your testimony here today, did you work a member of the Office of the Prosecutor's staff to create a list of all the names of the people who you recall were killed on this day in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, I said who those people were. I personally knew them, and I talked about them. I said it, and that's what was written down. I don't know how to explain it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this list read back to you and did you make any corrections or -- as it was read back to you, did you find it to be a correct --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It was correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you -- ask that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 430, tab 3, and I'd ask you, sir, do you recognise your writing on the bottom right-hand corner of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the list of names that was read to you in preparation of your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Are you going to read it out? I apologise. Is that what you said? Do you mean you're going to read it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to read it out now. I'm asking you was this the list that was read out to you prior to you signing in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I apologise. Yes, that is my signature, I did and everything is correct. All those people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time when you were reunited with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening, at about 7.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you find your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
utterances.text: I found them up by the village in a little cluster of trees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to return to your home and see what condition it was in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1701
